Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) that he recited ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," while in prayer. It was asked of him: "Do you add to the Qur'an?" He said: "No, but we were commanded with something, so I said it."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that he recited "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" in the Friday prayer, and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "I heard Ibn Umar reciting '﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾' and he said: 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.' Likewise it is in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b."

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he recited ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," while in prayer.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿فَجَعَلَهُ غُثَاءً﴾ (and made it into dark stubble): "He said: dry, crumbled herbage, ahwa, meaning changed (mutaghayyiran)."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to rehearse the Qur'an out of fear that he would forget it. So he was told: 'We have spared you that,' and the verse was revealed: ﴿سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلَا تَنْسَى﴾ (We will make you recite, so you will not forget)."

al-Hakim reported something similar from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿إِلَّا مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ (except what God wills) that he said: "Except what I will, so I will make you forget it."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding ﴿وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى﴾ (and We will ease you toward ease): "For the good."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى﴾: "Paradise."

al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾ (He has succeeded who purifies himself): "He who testifies that there is no god but God, abandons rivals, and testifies that I am the Messenger of God." Regarding ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾: "They are the five daily prayers, and guarding them and caring for their proper times."

al-Bazzar said: "It is not narrated from Jabir except through this route."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾: "From shirk." And ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ﴾: "He affirmed the oneness of God, and prayed." He said: "The five daily prayers."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾: "He who says: there is no god but God."

al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Kathir ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Awf, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "that he used to command the giving of zakat al-fitr before performing the Eid prayer, and would recite this verse: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾."

In another wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about zakat al-fitr, and he said: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾, and said: it is zakat al-fitr."

Kathir ibn Abd Allah is extremely weak. Abu Dawud said about him: "He is one of the pillars of falsehood." At-Tirmidhi authenticated a hadith through his route, but this was criticized. Yet what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri supports it, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾, then he would distribute the fitra before going out to the prayer-place on the day of Fitr." There is nothing in these two hadiths that indicates that this was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul); rather, they only state that he (ﷺ) recited the verse. His saying "it is zakat al-fitr" may mean that it is among the things to which the term "purification" (tazakki) applies. We have already noted that the surah is Meccan, and there was in Mecca neither an Eid prayer nor fitra.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri regarding ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾: "He gave the zakat al-fitr before he went out to the Eid." And ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾: "He went out to the Eid and prayed."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Umar, who said: "This verse was revealed only concerning the giving of zakat al-fitr before the Eid prayer: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾ ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ata, who said: "I said to Ibn Abbas: What do you think of His saying ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾ as being about the fitr?" He said: "I have not heard of that, but it is about all zakat." Then I returned to him and he said to me: "And all charities."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Arfaja al-Thaqafi, who said: "I asked Ibn Mas'ud to recite for me 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.' When he reached ﴿بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ he stopped reciting, turned to his companions, and said: 'We have preferred the world over the Hereafter.' The people were silent. Then he said: 'We have preferred the world because we saw its adornment, its women, its food, and its drink, and the Hereafter was hidden from us, so we chose this immediate thing and left the deferred one.'" And he recited (bal yu'thirun al-hayah al-dunya) with the letter ya'.

al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿إِنَّ هَذَا لَفِي الصُّحُفِ الْأُولَى صُحُفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَمُوسَى﴾: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'All of it is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him regarding the verse: "This surah was abrogated (nusikhat) from the scrolls of Abraham and Moses." In another wording: "This surah is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn Asakir reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, how many books did God send down?" He said: "A hundred books and four books." The hadith continues.

* *

(p-1614) Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Ghashiya was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh reported the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. The hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir has already been mentioned: "that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ and al-Ghashiya in the Eid prayer and on Friday."

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying: ﴿هَلْ أَتَاكَ حَدِيثُ الْغَاشِيَةِ﴾ (Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?) A group of exegetes said: "Hal" here means "qad" (indeed/already). Qutrub also said this: that is, "Indeed there has come to you, O Muhammad, the report of the Overwhelming," and it is the Resurrection, because it overwhelms creation with its terrors.

It was said that keeping "hal" here in its interrogative meaning, which implies amazement at its news and eagerness to hear it, is preferable.

Most exegetes went with the view that the Overwhelming here means the Resurrection.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "The Overwhelming is the Fire, which covers the faces of the disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿وَتَغْشَى وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ﴾ (and the Fire will cover their faces) [Ibrahim: 50]." It was also said: the Overwhelming is the people of the Fire, because they cover it and plunge into it. The first view is preferable.

al-Kalbi said: the meaning is: if the report of the Overwhelming has not come to you, then it has come to you now.

﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَاشِعَةٌ﴾ (Faces that day will be humbled). The clause is resumed (mustaʾnafa), answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What is it?" Or it is resumed in the grammatical sense of explaining what the event contains: that is, on that day there will be faces characterized by this described attribute. "Wujuh" (faces) is in the nominative as a subject, even though it is indefinite, because it occurs in a context of detail. A similar construction was mentioned before in surah al-Qiyama and surah al-Nazi'at.

The tanwin in "yawma'idhin" (that day) is a substitute for the omitted genitive: that is, the day of the coming of the Overwhelming. "Khashi'a" means humbled, subdued. Anything that is shrunken and still is called khashi'. It is said "khasha'a al-sawt" (the voice became low) when it became faint, and "khasha'a fi salatihi" (he became humble in his prayer) when he abased himself and lowered his head.

"Faces" here means their owners.

Muqatil said: he means the disbelievers, because they were arrogant toward worshipping God.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: humbled in the Fire. It was also said that he meant the faces of the Jews and Christians specifically.

The first view is preferable.

His saying: ﴿عَامِلَةٌ نَاصِبَةٌ﴾ (laboring, weary). The meaning of "laboring" is that they perform arduous work.

The people of linguistics said: it is said of a man when he persists in his journey: "'amila ya'malu 'amalan" (he labored), and it is said of a cloud when its lightning continues: "qad 'amila ya'malu 'amalan" (it has labored).

**It is said that this work is the dragging of chains and shackles and wading into the Fire.** *Nasibah* means weary, exhausted. It is said that *nasiba* (with kasra) *yansabu nasaban* means "he became weary." The meaning is that in the Hereafter they will be weary because of what they encounter of God's punishment.

It is also said that His words, *"working, toiling,"* refer to this world, since there is no work in the Hereafter. That is, they labor in this world in disbelief and sins, and they toil in that.

It is also said that they labor in this world and are weary in the Hereafter. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: ﴿Working, toiling﴾ means they were arrogant in this world toward obedience to God, so God made them labor and toil in the Fire, by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains ﴿on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they did not work for God in this world and did not toil, so He made them labor and toil in Jahannam.

Al-Kalbi said: they will be dragged on their faces in the Fire.

He also said: they will be commanded to climb a mountain of iron in Jahannam, and they will toil there with the greatest toil, handling chains and shackles and wading through the Fire as camels wade through mud.

The majority of readers (*qurra'*, reciters) read ﴿working, toiling﴾ in the nominative in both words, taking them as two further predicates of the subject, or as predicates of an implied subject. Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, Humayd and Ibn Kathir, in one report from him, read both in the accusative, as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*) or as an accusative of blame (*dhamm*).

His words ﴿burning in a scorching Fire﴾ are another predicate of the subject. That is, they enter a fire extremely intense in heat. It is said *hamiya al-nahar* and *hamiya al-tannur*, meaning the heat of both intensified.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is said *ishtadda hamy al-nahar* and *hamwuhu*, with the same meaning.

The majority read *tasla* with an open *ta'* as active voice. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read both *tusla* and the following word with a *damma* as passive voice. Abu Raja' read *tusla* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, an open *sad*, and a shadda on the *lam*. The pronoun refers to the faces in all these readings, and what is meant is their owners, as already mentioned.

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾. The "boiling spring" means one whose heat has reached its extreme. *Aniyah* means one whose heat has finished, from *al-iniya*, meaning delay. It is said *anahu yuniihi inaa'an*, meaning he delayed and detained him, as in His words: ﴿They will go around between it and a boiling hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said that if a single drop from it fell on the mountains of this world, they would melt.

When He, glorified be He, mentioned their drink, He followed it with mention of their food, saying: ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾. It is a kind of thorny plant called *al-shibriq* in the language of Quraysh while it is fresh, and when it dries it becomes *al-dari'*.

So said Mujahid, Qatadah and other commentators.

It is said that it is a deadly poison, and when it dries no animal approaches it or grazes on it. It is also said that it is something the sea casts up, called *al-dari'*, a food for livestock and not for people. If camels graze on it they are not sated and die of emaciation.

Al-Khalil said: *al-dari'* is a green plant with a foul smell that the sea casts up.

The majority of lexicographers and exegetes followed the first view, and from it comes the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*He grazed on the lush shibriq, until it withered and became dari', and the chaff fell away from it.*

Al-Hudhali, describing camels and the badness of their pasture, said:

*And confinement in the withered dari', while all of them are shorn-horned, with bleeding forelegs, scabby.*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: *al-dari'* is stones. It is also said it is a tree in the Fire of Jahannam.

Al-Hasan said: it is some of the punishment God has concealed.

Ibn Kaysan said: it is food at which they humble themselves, abase themselves, and beseech God for deliverance from it. It was named so because its eater beseeches God to be spared it, out of its loathing and roughness.

Al-Nahhas said: it may be derived from *al-dari'*, meaning the abject, that is, from drinking it he will be seized with humility and abasement.

Al-Hasan also said: it is *al-zaqqum*. It is also said it is a valley in Jahannam. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Haqqah: ﴿So today he has no friend here, nor any food except *ghislin*﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. *Al-ghislin* is other than *al-dari'*, as already mentioned. The two verses are reconciled by saying that the Fire has levels (*darakat*), so some have *al-dari'* as food and others have *al-ghislin* as food.

Then He, glorified be He, described *al-dari'*, saying: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. That is, *al-dari'* does not fatten its eater and does not remove the hunger that is in him.

The commentators said: when this verse was revealed, the polytheists said: "Our camels grow fat on *al-dari'*." So it was revealed: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. They lied in what they said, for camels do not eat *al-dari'* and do not approach it.

It is also said that the matter was confused for them, so they thought it was like other beneficial plants.

Then He, glorified be He, began to explain the state of the people of Paradise after finishing the explanation of the state of the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. That is, possessors of bliss and splendor. They are the faces of the believers, whose faces became radiant because of what they witnessed of the outcome of their affair and what God has prepared for them of good that surpasses description. A similar verse is His words: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24].

Then He said: ﴿Satisfied with their striving﴾. That is, satisfied with their deeds that they performed in this world, because they have been given a reward that pleased them and gladdened their eyes. The "faces" here means their owners, as already mentioned.

﴿In a lofty Garden﴾. That is, lofty in place, elevated above other places, or lofty in rank, because in it is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in.

﴿Where they will hear no vain talk﴾. The majority read *la tasma'u* with an open *ta'* and *laghiyah* in the accusative: that is, you, the addressee, will not hear, or those faces will not hear. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a *ya'* with a *damma* in the passive voice and *laghiyatun* in the nominative. Nafi' read it with a *ta'* with a *damma* in the passive voice and *laghiyatun* in the nominative. Al-Fadl and al-Ja'dari read it with an open *ya'* in the active voice and *laghiyah* in the accusative. *Al-laghw* is falling speech.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: that is, you will not hear in it a word of vain talk.

It is said the meaning is lying, falsehood and disbelief. Qatadah said this, and Mujahid said: that is, reviling.

Al-Farra' said: you will not hear in it one who swears an oath with a lie.

Al-Kalbi said: you will not hear in Paradise one who swears an oath, whether righteous or sinful.

Al-Farra' also said: you will not hear in the speech of the people of Paradise a word that is vain, because they speak only with wisdom and praise of God for what He has granted them of lasting bliss. This is the most preferred of the views, because an indefinite noun in the context of negation is a form of generality, and there is no basis for restricting it to a particular kind of vain talk unless there is a specifier suitable for restriction.

*Laghiyah* is either an adjective of an omitted noun, that is, a word that is vain (*kalimah laghiyah*), or a soul that is vain (*nafs laghiyah*), or a verbal noun, that is, you will not hear in it *laghwan* (vain talk).

﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Insan that in it are springs. *Al-'ayn* here means the plural *'uyun*, as in His words: ﴿A soul will know﴾ [al-Takwir: 14]. The meaning of *jariyah* (flowing) is that its waters flow and gush forth with kinds of delicious drinks.

Al-Kalbi said: I do not know whether it is water or something else.

﴿In it are raised couches﴾. That is, lofty and elevated in height, or lofty in rank.

﴿And cups set in place﴾. It has already been mentioned that *al-akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which is a cup without a handle. The meaning of *mawdu'ah* (set in place) is that they are placed before them, from which they drink.

﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾. *Al-namariq* are cushions.

Al-Wahidi said: by the agreement of all, its singular is *numruqah* with a *damma* on the *nun*. Al-Farra' added, from Arabic hearing, *nimriqah* with a *kasra*.

Al-Kalbi said: cushions arranged in rows, some next to others. From it is the verse of the poet:

*And indeed we pass the cup among our drinkers, and between Abu Qabus, above the cushions.*

Another said:

*Elders and young men, fair of face, on couches arranged in rows, and cushions.*

In *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari) it says: *al-numruq* and *al-nimriqah* are a small cushion, and likewise *al-nimriqah* with a *kasra* is a dialectal form related by Ya'qub.

﴿And carpets spread out﴾. That is, rugs. Its singular is *zurbi* and *zurbiyyah*.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: *al-zarabi* are the thin-piled carpets (*tanafis*) with a fine nap, and its singular is *zarbiyyah*. *Mabthuthah* means spread out. So said Qatadah.

Ikrimah said: some of them are above others.

Al-Wahidi said: it may also mean that they are scattered in the gatherings. Al-Qutaybi said the same.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning of *mabthuthah* is many. The apparent meaning of *al-bath* is scattering together with abundance, and from it is His words: ﴿And He scattered throughout it from every creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied element, as in its parallels that have passed more than once. The sentence is directed to establish the matter of resurrection and to argue for it, and so is what follows. *Kayfa* is accusative, governed by what follows it. The clause is in the genitive position as a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion, a substitute that comprises part of the meaning of the noun it replaces) for *al-ibil* (the camels). The meaning is: do they deny the matter of resurrection and consider its occurrence unlikely? Do they not look at the camels, which are the mainstay of their livestock and the greatest of the created things they witness, ﴿how they were created﴾ in the wonderful form they have, with the greatness of their bodies, the abundance of their strength, and the wonder of their attributes?

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: he singled out the camels because they are among the quadrupeds that kneel, so that loads can be put on them, whereas other quadrupeds are not loaded unless they are standing. Al-Zajjaj said: He drew their attention to a great creature of His creation which He has made subservient to the little one, who leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and loads it with heavy burdens while it is kneeling. It then rises with the weight of its load, and no other load-bearing animal does this. So He showed them a great part of His creation, to indicate by it His unity.

Al-Hasan was asked about this verse, and it was said to him: the elephant is more wondrous. He said: as for the elephant, the Arabs are far removed from it. Moreover it is a pig (*khinzir*) whose back is not ridden, whose meat is not eaten, and whose milk is not milked. The camel is among the most precious and valuable property of the Arabs. It eats date-stones and fodder, produces milk, and a child takes hold of its halter and leads it wherever he wishes, despite its great size in itself.

Al-Mubarrad said: the camels here are the great clouds of the sky, but this differs from what the commentators and lexicographers mentioned.

It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: whoever reads *khuliqat* with a light pronunciation means the camel, and whoever reads it with a shadda means the clouds.

﴿And at the sky, how it was raised﴾. That is, it was raised above the earth without pillars, in a manner that understanding cannot grasp and reason cannot comprehend. It is also said: it was raised so that nothing can reach it.

﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm﴾ upon the earth, fixed and firm, not swaying, not leaning, and not moving.

﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out﴾. That is, it was spread. *Al-sath* is the spreading of a thing. It is said of the roof of a house when it is level: *sath*.

The majority read *suthihat* in the passive voice with a light pronunciation. Al-Hasan read it with a shadda. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu al-'Aliyah read *khalaqtu, rafa'tu, nasabtu, sathahtu* (I created, I raised, I set, I spread) in the active voice with a *damma* on the *ta'* in all of them, as a first-person address from God.

Then He, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to remind, saying: ﴿So remind﴾. The *fa'* indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes. That is: so admonish them, O Muhammad, and warn them. Then He gave the reason for the command to remind, saying: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾. That is, nothing is incumbent upon you except that.

﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. *Al-musaytir* and *al-musayтир* with *sin* and *sad* mean one who is given power over a thing in order to oversee it and attend to its affairs, as stated in *al-Sihah*. That is: you are not over them a controller, so that you compel them to faith. This verse has been abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e., its ruling superseded by a later revelation) by the verse of the sword.

The majority read *bi-musaytir* with *sad*. Hisham and Qunbul in one report read it with *sin*. Khalaf read it with the *sad* pronounced as *za'* (the sound of *sad* mixed with *zay*). Harun al-A'war read it with an open *ta'* as a passive participle.

﴿Except for him who turns away and disbelieves﴾. This is an exception of disconnection (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes): that is, but as for he who turns away from admonition and reminder...

﴿فَيُعَذِّبُهُ اللَّهُ الْعَذَابَ الْأَكْبَرَ﴾ ("then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment"). This is the lasting punishment of Hell (Jahannam). It is also said that this is an exception (istithna' muttasil, a connected exception) from His saying "so remind," meaning: remind everyone except the one whose hope of his faith has been cut off and who turned away, so he deserves the greatest punishment. The first view is preferable.

It is called "the greatest" because they were already punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "فَإنَّهُ يُعَذِّبُهُ اللَّهُ" ("then indeed Allah will punish him"). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah recited "أَلَا مَنْ تَوَلَّى" ("Unquestionably, whoever turns away"), taking "ألا" as the particle of alerting and opening (lil-tanbih wal-istiftah).

﴿إنَّ إلَيْنا إيابَهُمْ﴾ ("Indeed, to Us is their return"), meaning their return after death. It is said: "āba yaūbu" when one returns. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"Every absent one returns, but the absent one of death does not return."

The majority read "إيابَهم" with light stress (takhfif). Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with a doubled letter (tashdid). Abu Hatim said: tashdid is not permissible; if it were, its equivalent would be permissible in "al-siyam" and "al-qiyam." It is also said that both are dialectal variants with the same meaning.

Al-Wahidi said: As for "إيابَهم" with a doubled yā', it is anomalous (shadh), and no one permitted it except al-Zajjaj.

﴿ثُمَّ إنَّ عَلَيْنا حِسابَهُمْ﴾ ("Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning"), meaning their recompense after their return to Allah through resurrection. "Thumma" here indicates a delay in rank, because the station of reckoning is far greater in severity than the station of return.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-Ghashiyah" is one of the names of the Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿هَلْ أتاكَ حَدِيثُ الغاشِيَةِ﴾ ("Has there come to you the news of the Overwhelming?"), that he said: "It is the Hour." Regarding ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خاشِعَةٌ عامِلَةٌ ناصِبَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring, weary"), he said: "They will labour and be weary in the Fire." Regarding ﴿تُسْقى مِن عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ﴾ ("They will be given drink from a boiling spring"), he said: "It is the one whose heat has reached its limit." Regarding ﴿لَيْسَ لَهم طَعامٌ إلّا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾ ("They will have no food except from a thorny plant"), he said: "It is al-shibriq."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: Regarding ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خاشِعَةٌ عامِلَةٌ ناصِبَةٌ﴾, he said: "It means the Jews and the Christians; they are humbled, but their deeds will not benefit them." Regarding ﴿تُسْقى مِن عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ﴾, he said: "Its boiling has reached its peak."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His saying ﴿تَصْلى نارًا حامِيَةً﴾ ("They will burn in a scorching Fire"), that he said: "Intensely hot." Regarding ﴿تُسْقى مِن عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ﴾, he said: "Its heat has ended." Regarding ﴿لَيْسَ لَهم طَعامٌ إلّا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾, he said: "From a tree of fire."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him also regarding ﴿إلّا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾, that he said: "Dried al-shibriq."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also regarding ﴿لا تَسْمَعُ فِيها لاغِيَةً﴾ ("They will not hear therein any vain talk"), that he said: "They will not hear harm or falsehood." Regarding ﴿فِيها سُرُرٌ مَرْفُوعَةٌ﴾ ("Therein are couches raised high"), he said: "Some of them above others." Regarding ﴿ونَمارِقُ﴾ ("and cushions arranged"), he said: "Sitting places."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding ﴿ونَمارِقُ﴾, that he said: "Armrests."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding ﴿لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ﴾ ("You are not over them a controller"), that he said: "A tyrant." Regarding ﴿إلّا مَن تَوَلّى وكَفَرَ﴾ ("But whoever turns away and disbelieves"), he said: "His reckoning is upon Allah."

Abu Dawud, in his book on abrogation (al-nasikh, the verses that abrogate others), narrated from him also regarding ﴿لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ﴾ that this was then abrogated by His saying: ﴿فَاقْتُلُوا المُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ ("Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them") [al-Tawbah: 5].

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him also regarding ﴿إنَّ إلَيْنا إيابَهُمْ﴾ that he said: "Their return."

This surah is Meccan according to the majority of scholars.
Al-Dahhak said: it is Madani.
Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The surah "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" was revealed in Mecca.
Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAʾishah something similar.
Al-Bukhari and others related from al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib that he said: "The first of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ to come to us was Mus'ab ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, and they began teaching us the Qur'an. Then ʿAmmar, Bilal and Saʿd came. Then ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab came with twenty men. Then the Prophet ﷺ came, and I have never seen the people of Medina rejoice at anything as much as they rejoiced at him, until I saw the young girls and boys saying: 'This is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who has come.' He had not arrived until I recited 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High' in a surah like it."
Ahmad, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿAli that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ loved this surah: 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.'"
Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Sunan related from al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite in the two ʿEids and on Friday 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High' and 'Has there come to you the narration of the Overwhelming (al-Ghashiyah)?' And if the day coincided with Friday he recited both of them together." In another wording: "Sometimes both came together on one day, and he recited them both." There are other hadiths on this subject.
Muslim and others related from Jabir ibn Samurah that "the Prophet ﷺ used to recite 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High' in the Zuhr prayer."
Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray Witr with 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,' 'Say: O disbelievers,' and 'Say: He is Allah, One.'"
Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi related from ʿAʾishah that she said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the Witr prayer, in the first rak'ah, 'Glorify,' in the second 'Say: O disbelievers,' and in the third 'Say: He is Allah, One' and the two refuges (al-Mu'awwidhatayn)." In the Two Sahihs it is related that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Mu'adh: 'Why did you not pray with "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High," "By the sun and its brightness," and "By the night when it covers" [i.e., Surat al-Layl]?'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: declare Him free of everything that is not fitting for Him.
Al-Suddi said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: magnify Him. It has been said that "name" here is superfluous, used for the purpose of exalting, as in the verse of Labid:
"Until the year is complete, then peace be upon you both; and whoever weeps for a full year has indeed made an excuse."
The meaning is: glorify your Lord, the Most High.
Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is, declare the name of your Lord free from being named by anyone other than Him, so on this view it is not superfluous.
It has been said the meaning is: declare the naming of your Lord and your mention of Him free from being mentioned except by one who is humble and reverent, and whose remembrance of Him is respected.
Al-Hasan said: the meaning of "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" is: pray to Him.
It has been said the meaning is: pray with the names of Allah, not as the polytheists pray with whistling and clapping.
It has been said the meaning is: raise your voice in remembrance of your Lord. From this is the saying of Jarir:
"May God disfigure the faces of Taghlib whenever the pilgrims glorify and proclaim the takbir in full."
"The Most High" is an attribute of the Lord; it has been said it is an attribute of the name, and the first is preferable.
His saying ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ is another attribute of the Lord.
Al-Zajjaj said: He created man upright, and the meaning of "proportioned" is that He made his stature balanced.
Al-Dahhak said: He created him and proportioned his creation. It has been said He created the bodies and proportioned the understandings; it has been said He created man and prepared him for legal responsibility.
﴿And who decreed and guided﴾ is another attribute of the Lord, or is conjoined to the relative clause before it.
ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Kisa'i and al-Sulami read "qadar" (decreed) with light pronunciation, and the rest read it with doubling (qaddara). Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: He decreed the creation of male and female among the animals, and guided the male to the female, how he should approach her.
Mujahid said: He guided man to the path of good and evil, and of happiness and misery.
It is also related from him that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: He decreed happiness and misery, and guided to right guidance and error, and guided the cattle to their pasture.
It has been said He decreed their provisions and sustenance, and guided them to their livelihood if they are humans, and to their pasture if they are wild beasts.
ʿAṭa' said: For every creature was made what sustains it, and He guided it to it.
It has been said He created the benefits in things and guided man to the way of extracting them from them.
Al-Suddi said: He decreed the period of the fetus in the womb as nine months, or less or more, then guided it to leave the womb.
Al-Farra' said: That is, He decreed and guided, and He misguided; so one of the two was mentioned alone. There are views on the interpretation of the verse other than what we have mentioned.
The preferable course is not to specify a single individual or individuals from among what the words "decreed" and "guided" may apply to, except by a proof that indicates it. Where there is no proof, it is to be understood as applying to the meaning of both verbs, either by substitution or by generality. The meaning is: He decreed the kinds of things, their types, their attributes, their actions, their sayings, and their terms, then guided each of them to what proceeds from it and what befits it, facilitated for it what it was created for, and inspired it with the matters of its religion and its worldly life.
And ﴿Who brought forth the pasture﴾ is another attribute of the Lord: that is, He caused to grow the herbage and the plants that cattle graze, the green vegetation.
﴿Then made it dark stubble﴾: that is, after it was green He made it stubble, dry chaff like the debris that is carried on top of a flood. ﴿Dark﴾: that is, black after being green, for when the grass dries it turns black.
Qatadah said: "Ghuthaʾ" is dry matter; it is said of herbs and grass when they are broken and dried: ghuthaʾ and hashim (dry stalks).
Imru' al-Qays said:
"As if the tops of the head of al-Mujaymir in the morning, from the flood and the debris, were a spindle-whorl."
The accusative of "ghuthaʾ" is either as the second object, or as a circumstantial state, and "dark" (ahwa) is its attribute.
Al-Kisa'i said: it is a state of "the pasture": that is, He brought it forth dark from the intensity of its greenness and moisture, then after that made it stubble. "Ahwa" is derived from "hiwwa," which is a blackness that inclines toward green.
In al-Sihah it is said: "hiwwa" is the darkness of the lip (dark lip), and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:
"Lamiyya, in whose lips is a dark sweetness, and in the gums and in the teeth is a sweet purity (shanab)."
﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾: that is, We shall make you a reciter by inspiring you with recitation, so you will not forget what you recite. The sentence is resumptive, explaining his special guidance ﷺ after the general guidance; it is his guidance ﷺ to memorize the Qur'an.
Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: "When Gabriel came to the Prophet ﷺ with revelation, Gabriel would not finish the last of the verse before the Prophet ﷺ began to speak its first part, for fear that he would forget it. So ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ was revealed."
His saying ﴿except what Allah wills﴾ is an exception of the type "mufarragh" from the most general of the objects: that is, you will not forget any of the things you recite except what Allah wills that you forget.
Al-Farra' said: He, glory be to Him, did not will that Muhammad ﷺ forget anything, like His saying: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. It has been said: except what Allah wills that you forget and then you remember afterward; so he forgets but then remembers, and does not forget anything with a total forgetting.
It has been said it means abrogation: that is, except what Allah wills to abrogate of its recitation.
It has been said the meaning of "you will not forget" is: you will not abandon acting upon it, except what Allah wills that you abandon, by its abrogation and the lifting of its ruling.
It has been said the meaning is: except what Allah wills to delay its sending down.
It has been said the "lā" in His saying "fa-lā tansā" is a prohibition. The alif is added for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila), as in His saying: ﴿fa-aḍallūnā as-sabīlā﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]. That is: do not neglect its recitation, and remember it.
﴿Indeed He knows what is spoken aloud and what is hidden﴾: this sentence gives a reason for what precedes it: that is, He knows what is apparent and what is concealed, and the open and the secret. Its apparent meaning is generality, so there falls under it what has been said: that "what is spoken aloud" is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ memorized of the Qur'an, and "what is hidden" is what was abrogated from his breast. There also falls under it what has been said: that "what is spoken aloud" is the public declaration of charity and "what is hidden" is its concealment. There also falls under it what has been said: that "what is spoken aloud" is his ﷺ loud recitation of the Qur'an together with Gabriel's recitation, for fear that it would slip from him, and "what is hidden" is what is in his soul that prompts him to loud recitation.
﴿And We shall ease you toward ease﴾ is coordinated with "We shall make you recite," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause.
Muqatil said: that is, We make easy for you the work of Paradise. It has been said: We grant you success in the way that is easier and simpler. It has been said: to the easy sharia, which is the simple Hanifiyyah. It has been said: We make easy for you the revelation until you memorize it and act upon it. The preferable course is to understand the verse in its generality: that is, We grant you success in the easy path in religion and in worldly life, in every matter of theirs that is directed toward you.
﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾: that is, admonish, O Muhammad, the people with what We have revealed to you, guide them to the paths of good, and direct them to the laws of the religion.
Al-Hasan said: It is a reminder for the believer and a proof against the disbeliever.
Al-Wahidi said: "if it benefits or does not benefit" — he did not mention the second case, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and so on.
Al-Jurjani said: admonition is obligatory even if it does not benefit; so the meaning is: "if the reminder benefits, or does not benefit."
It has been said that it is specific to particular people. It has been said: "in" here means "mā," that is: remind, since the reminder is beneficial in every case. It has been said it means "qad," and it has been said it means "idh."
What al-Wahidi and al-Jurjani said is preferable, and al-Farra' and al-Nahhas had preceded them in this view.
Al-Razi said: His saying "if the reminder benefits" points to the more noble of the two states, namely the existence of the benefit for the sake of which the reminder was prescribed; and what is conditioned by "in" on something does not necessarily mean its non-existence when that thing is absent. Several verses show this: among them this verse; among them His saying: ﴿and give thanks to Allah, if it is Him you worship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]; among them His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa': 101], for shortening is permissible both in fear and in its absence; and among them His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon them if they return to one another, if they think they can keep the limits of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], for return is permissible without this supposition. So this condition has benefits: among them what has preceded, and among them the urging to benefit from the reminder, as a man says to one he is guiding: "I have made it clear to you, if you understand." It is also an alert to the Prophet ﷺ that the reminder will not benefit them; or this applies to the repetition of the call, whereas the first call is general. End of quotation.

Then He, glory be to Him, distinguished between one who benefits from the reminder and one who does not, saying: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾, that is: whoever fears Allah will be admonished by your exhortation, and through the reminder his fear and righteousness will increase.
﴿And the most wretched will avoid it﴾, that is: the most wretched of the disbelievers will avoid and keep far from the reminder, due to his persistence in disbelief in Allah and his immersion in His disobedience.
Then He described the most wretched, saying: ﴿who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾, that is, the great and dreadful one, because it is more intense in heat than others.
Al-Hasan said: "The greatest Fire" is the Fire of Hell, and "the lesser Fire" is the fire of this world.
Al-Zajjaj said: it is the lowest of the layers of the Fire.
﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live﴾: that is, he will not die in it so as to rest from the punishment he is in, nor will he live a life from which he benefits. From this is the saying of the poet:
"Oh, for a soul that does not die so that its woe may end, nor live a life that has any sweetness."
"Then" (thumma) indicates a gradation in the degrees of severity, because wavering between death and life is more dreadful than burning in the greatest Fire.
﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾, that is: whoever purifies himself from polytheism, believes in Allah, affirms His oneness, and acts according to His laws.
ʿAṭa' and al-Rabi' said: whoever's deed is pure and growing.
Qatadah said: he purifies himself by righteous deed.
Qatadah, ʿAṭa' and Abu al-ʿAliyah said: it was revealed concerning the zakat al-fitr.
ʿIkrimah said: a man would say, "I present my zakat before my prayer."
The root meaning of zakah in the language is growth.
It has been said the verse intends the zakat of all wealth.
It has been said it intends the purification of deeds, not the zakat of wealth, because the more common usage for wealth is "zakka" and not "tazakka."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 88, verses 1–26 (part 2 of 4):

﴿وذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلّى﴾ It was said the meaning is: he remembered the name of his Lord with fear, so he worshipped Him and prayed to Him. It was also said: he remembered the name of his Lord with his tongue, and prayed, that is, he performed the five daily prayers (al-salawat al-khams).

It was said: he remembered his standing before Him and his return to Him, so he worshipped Him. This is like the first saying.

It was said: he remembered the name of his Lord by saying the takbir at the beginning of the prayer, because the prayer is not validly begun except with His remembrance, which is His saying: "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest). It was said: he remembered the name of his Lord on the way to the prayer-place and then prayed. It was said: it means that he performs a voluntary prayer after giving charity (zakat).

It was said: the prayer here means the Eid prayer (salat al-'id), just as the purification (tazakki) in the first verse means zakat al-fitr (the obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan). But this saying is far-fetched, because the surah is Meccan, and zakat al-fitr and the Eid prayer were only made obligatory in Medina.

﴿بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الحَياةَ الدُّنْيا﴾ Rather, you prefer the worldly life. This is a turning away (idrab) from an implied statement that the context indicates: that is, you do not do this, but rather you prefer the fleeting pleasures of the world.

The majority of readers (al-jumhur) read tu'thirun with the letter ta' (second person, "you prefer"), and the reading of Ubayy supports it: "bal antum tu'thirun" (rather, you yourselves prefer). Abu Amr read it with the letter ya' (third person, "they prefer").

It was said: the verse refers to the disbelievers, and preferring the worldly life means being content with it, relying on it, and completely turning away from the Hereafter. It was also said: it refers to all people, believers and disbelievers, and preferring the world means something more general, which most people are not free from: the influence of the worldly side over the Hereafter, turning toward gaining its benefits, and caring for it more than for acts of obedience.

﴿وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى﴾ And the Hereafter is better and more lasting. It is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of tu'thirun, meaning: while the fact is that the Abode of the Hereafter, which is Paradise, is better and more lasting than the world. Malik ibn Dinar said: "If the world were gold that perishes, and the Hereafter were pottery that endures, it would be obligatory to prefer the pottery that endures over the gold that perishes. How much more so when the Hereafter is gold that endures and the world is pottery that perishes!"

﴿إِنَّ هَذَا لَفِي الصُّحُفِ الْأُولَى * صُحُفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَمُوسَى﴾ The reference in "Indeed, this" is to what preceded: the success of the one who purifies himself and what follows it. It was also said that it refers to the whole surah. The meaning of "in the former scriptures" is: it is established in them.

"The scrolls of Abraham and Moses" is an apposition (badal) to "the former scriptures."

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: by his saying "Indeed, this" he means: "and the Hereafter is better and more lasting." They said: the books of God, Mighty and Majestic, have agreed (tata'bi'at) that the Hereafter is better and more lasting than the world.

Al-Hasan said: the books of God, Mighty is His praise, have agreed that "Indeed, this is in the former scriptures," which is His saying: "He has succeeded..." to the end of the surah.

The majority read "fi al-suhuf al-ula suhufi Ibrahim" with a damma on the ha' (ḥāʾ) in both places. Al-A'mash, Harun, and Abu Amr in one narration from him read them with sukun on it in both places. The majority read "Ibrahim" with an alif after the ra' and a ya' after the ha'. Abu Raja read it without them and with a fatha on the ha'. Abu Musa and Ibn al-Zubayr read "Ibrahamu" with two alifs.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Uqba ibn Amir al-Juhani, who said: "When the verse ﴿فَسَبِّحْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ [al-Haqqa: 52] (So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty) was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to us: 'Make it in your bowing (ruku').' When the verse ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ (Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High) was revealed, [i.e., the surah al-A'la], he said: 'Make it in your prostration (sujud).'" There is no objection to its chain of narration.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Abbas that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he recited ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ would say: 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.'"

Abu Dawud said: "Waki' opposed him in this; Shu'ba narrated it from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas, as a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf)."

It was also reported as a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf) by Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir: that when he recited "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High," he would say: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." In a wording of Abd ibn Humayd from him: "When you recite 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,' say: 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.'"

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) that he recited ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," while in prayer. It was asked of him: "Do you add to the Qur'an?" He said: "No, but we were commanded with something, so I said it."

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that he recited "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High" in the Friday prayer, and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "I heard Ibn Umar reciting '﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾' and he said: 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.' Likewise it is in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b."

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that he recited ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," while in prayer.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿فَجَعَلَهُ غُثَاءً﴾ (and made it into dark stubble): "He said: dry, crumbled herbage, ahwa, meaning changed (mutaghayyiran)."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to rehearse the Qur'an out of fear that he would forget it. So he was told: 'We have spared you that,' and the verse was revealed: ﴿سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلَا تَنْسَى﴾ (We will make you recite, so you will not forget)."

al-Hakim reported something similar from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿إِلَّا مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ﴾ (except what God wills) that he said: "Except what I will, so I will make you forget it."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding ﴿وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى﴾ (and We will ease you toward ease): "For the good."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى﴾: "Paradise."

al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾ (He has succeeded who purifies himself): "He who testifies that there is no god but God, abandons rivals, and testifies that I am the Messenger of God." Regarding ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾: "They are the five daily prayers, and guarding them and caring for their proper times."

al-Bazzar said: "It is not narrated from Jabir except through this route."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾: "From shirk." And ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ﴾: "He affirmed the oneness of God, and prayed." He said: "The five daily prayers."

al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾: "He who says: there is no god but God."

al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Kathir ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Awf, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "that he used to command the giving of zakat al-fitr before performing the Eid prayer, and would recite this verse: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾."

In another wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about zakat al-fitr, and he said: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾, and said: it is zakat al-fitr."

Kathir ibn Abd Allah is extremely weak. Abu Dawud said about him: "He is one of the pillars of falsehood." At-Tirmidhi authenticated a hadith through his route, but this was criticized. Yet what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri supports it, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾, then he would distribute the fitra before going out to the prayer-place on the day of Fitr." There is nothing in these two hadiths that indicates that this was the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul); rather, they only state that he (ﷺ) recited the verse. His saying "it is zakat al-fitr" may mean that it is among the things to which the term "purification" (tazakki) applies. We have already noted that the surah is Meccan, and there was in Mecca neither an Eid prayer nor fitra.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri regarding ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾: "He gave the zakat al-fitr before he went out to the Eid." And ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾: "He went out to the Eid and prayed."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Umar, who said: "This verse was revealed only concerning the giving of zakat al-fitr before the Eid prayer: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾ ﴿وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ata, who said: "I said to Ibn Abbas: What do you think of His saying ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى﴾ as being about the fitr?" He said: "I have not heard of that, but it is about all zakat." Then I returned to him and he said to me: "And all charities."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Arfaja al-Thaqafi, who said: "I asked Ibn Mas'ud to recite for me 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.' When he reached ﴿بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ he stopped reciting, turned to his companions, and said: 'We have preferred the world over the Hereafter.' The people were silent. Then he said: 'We have preferred the world because we saw its adornment, its women, its food, and its drink, and the Hereafter was hidden from us, so we chose this immediate thing and left the deferred one.'" And he recited (bal yu'thirun al-hayah al-dunya) with the letter ya'.

al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿إِنَّ هَذَا لَفِي الصُّحُفِ الْأُولَى صُحُفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَمُوسَى﴾: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'All of it is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him regarding the verse: "This surah was abrogated (nusikhat) from the scrolls of Abraham and Moses." In another wording: "This surah is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn Asakir reported from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, how many books did God send down?" He said: "A hundred books and four books." The hadith continues.

* *

(p-1614) Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Ghashiya was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh reported the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. The hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir has already been mentioned: "that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَى﴾ and al-Ghashiya in the Eid prayer and on Friday."

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

His saying: ﴿هَلْ أَتَاكَ حَدِيثُ الْغَاشِيَةِ﴾ (Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?) A group of exegetes said: "Hal" here means "qad" (indeed/already). Qutrub also said this: that is, "Indeed there has come to you, O Muhammad, the report of the Overwhelming," and it is the Resurrection, because it overwhelms creation with its terrors.

It was said that keeping "hal" here in its interrogative meaning, which implies amazement at its news and eagerness to hear it, is preferable.

Most exegetes went with the view that the Overwhelming here means the Resurrection.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "The Overwhelming is the Fire, which covers the faces of the disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿وَتَغْشَى وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ﴾ (and the Fire will cover their faces) [Ibrahim: 50]." It was also said: the Overwhelming is the people of the Fire, because they cover it and plunge into it. The first view is preferable.

al-Kalbi said: the meaning is: if the report of the Overwhelming has not come to you, then it has come to you now.

﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَاشِعَةٌ﴾ (Faces that day will be humbled). The clause is resumed (mustaʾnafa), answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What is it?" Or it is resumed in the grammatical sense of explaining what the event contains: that is, on that day there will be faces characterized by this described attribute. "Wujuh" (faces) is in the nominative as a subject, even though it is indefinite, because it occurs in a context of detail. A similar construction was mentioned before in surah al-Qiyama and surah al-Nazi'at.

The tanwin in "yawma'idhin" (that day) is a substitute for the omitted genitive: that is, the day of the coming of the Overwhelming. "Khashi'a" means humbled, subdued. Anything that is shrunken and still is called khashi'. It is said "khasha'a al-sawt" (the voice became low) when it became faint, and "khasha'a fi salatihi" (he became humble in his prayer) when he abased himself and lowered his head.

"Faces" here means their owners.

Muqatil said: he means the disbelievers, because they were arrogant toward worshipping God.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: humbled in the Fire. It was also said that he meant the faces of the Jews and Christians specifically.

The first view is preferable.

His saying: ﴿عَامِلَةٌ نَاصِبَةٌ﴾ (laboring, weary). The meaning of "laboring" is that they perform arduous work.

The people of linguistics said: it is said of a man when he persists in his journey: "'amila ya'malu 'amalan" (he labored), and it is said of a cloud when its lightning continues: "qad 'amila ya'malu 'amalan" (it has labored).

**It is said that this work is the dragging of chains and shackles and wading into the Fire.** *Nasibah* means weary, exhausted. It is said that *nasiba* (with kasra) *yansabu nasaban* means "he became weary." The meaning is that in the Hereafter they will be weary because of what they encounter of God's punishment.

It is also said that His words, *"working, toiling,"* refer to this world, since there is no work in the Hereafter. That is, they labor in this world in disbelief and sins, and they toil in that.

It is also said that they labor in this world and are weary in the Hereafter. The first view is preferable.

Qatadah said: ﴿Working, toiling﴾ means they were arrogant in this world toward obedience to God, so God made them labor and toil in the Fire, by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains ﴿on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they did not work for God in this world and did not toil, so He made them labor and toil in Jahannam.

Al-Kalbi said: they will be dragged on their faces in the Fire.

He also said: they will be commanded to climb a mountain of iron in Jahannam, and they will toil there with the greatest toil, handling chains and shackles and wading through the Fire as camels wade through mud.

The majority of readers (*qurra'*, reciters) read ﴿working, toiling﴾ in the nominative in both words, taking them as two further predicates of the subject, or as predicates of an implied subject. Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, Humayd and Ibn Kathir, in one report from him, read both in the accusative, as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*) or as an accusative of blame (*dhamm*).

His words ﴿burning in a scorching Fire﴾ are another predicate of the subject. That is, they enter a fire extremely intense in heat. It is said *hamiya al-nahar* and *hamiya al-tannur*, meaning the heat of both intensified.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is said *ishtadda hamy al-nahar* and *hamwuhu*, with the same meaning.

The majority read *tasla* with an open *ta'* as active voice. Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read both *tusla* and the following word with a *damma* as passive voice. Abu Raja' read *tusla* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, an open *sad*, and a shadda on the *lam*. The pronoun refers to the faces in all these readings, and what is meant is their owners, as already mentioned.

﴿They will be given drink from a boiling spring﴾. The "boiling spring" means one whose heat has reached its extreme. *Aniyah* means one whose heat has finished, from *al-iniya*, meaning delay. It is said *anahu yuniihi inaa'an*, meaning he delayed and detained him, as in His words: ﴿They will go around between it and a boiling hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44]. Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said that if a single drop from it fell on the mountains of this world, they would melt.

When He, glorified be He, mentioned their drink, He followed it with mention of their food, saying: ﴿They will have no food except from *dari'*﴾. It is a kind of thorny plant called *al-shibriq* in the language of Quraysh while it is fresh, and when it dries it becomes *al-dari'*.

So said Mujahid, Qatadah and other commentators.

It is said that it is a deadly poison, and when it dries no animal approaches it or grazes on it. It is also said that it is something the sea casts up, called *al-dari'*, a food for livestock and not for people. If camels graze on it they are not sated and die of emaciation.

Al-Khalil said: *al-dari'* is a green plant with a foul smell that the sea casts up.

The majority of lexicographers and exegetes followed the first view, and from it comes the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*He grazed on the lush shibriq, until it withered and became dari', and the chaff fell away from it.*

Al-Hudhali, describing camels and the badness of their pasture, said:

*And confinement in the withered dari', while all of them are shorn-horned, with bleeding forelegs, scabby.*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: *al-dari'* is stones. It is also said it is a tree in the Fire of Jahannam.

Al-Hasan said: it is some of the punishment God has concealed.

Ibn Kaysan said: it is food at which they humble themselves, abase themselves, and beseech God for deliverance from it. It was named so because its eater beseeches God to be spared it, out of its loathing and roughness.

Al-Nahhas said: it may be derived from *al-dari'*, meaning the abject, that is, from drinking it he will be seized with humility and abasement.

Al-Hasan also said: it is *al-zaqqum*. It is also said it is a valley in Jahannam. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Haqqah: ﴿So today he has no friend here, nor any food except *ghislin*﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. *Al-ghislin* is other than *al-dari'*, as already mentioned. The two verses are reconciled by saying that the Fire has levels (*darakat*), so some have *al-dari'* as food and others have *al-ghislin* as food.

Then He, glorified be He, described *al-dari'*, saying: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. That is, *al-dari'* does not fatten its eater and does not remove the hunger that is in him.

The commentators said: when this verse was revealed, the polytheists said: "Our camels grow fat on *al-dari'*." So it was revealed: ﴿It neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger﴾. They lied in what they said, for camels do not eat *al-dari'* and do not approach it.

It is also said that the matter was confused for them, so they thought it was like other beneficial plants.

Then He, glorified be He, began to explain the state of the people of Paradise after finishing the explanation of the state of the people of the Fire, saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾. That is, possessors of bliss and splendor. They are the faces of the believers, whose faces became radiant because of what they witnessed of the outcome of their affair and what God has prepared for them of good that surpasses description. A similar verse is His words: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 24].

Then He said: ﴿Satisfied with their striving﴾. That is, satisfied with their deeds that they performed in this world, because they have been given a reward that pleased them and gladdened their eyes. The "faces" here means their owners, as already mentioned.

﴿In a lofty Garden﴾. That is, lofty in place, elevated above other places, or lofty in rank, because in it is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in.

﴿Where they will hear no vain talk﴾. The majority read *la tasma'u* with an open *ta'* and *laghiyah* in the accusative: that is, you, the addressee, will not hear, or those faces will not hear. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a *ya'* with a *damma* in the passive voice and *laghiyatun* in the nominative. Nafi' read it with a *ta'* with a *damma* in the passive voice and *laghiyatun* in the nominative. Al-Fadl and al-Ja'dari read it with an open *ya'* in the active voice and *laghiyah* in the accusative. *Al-laghw* is falling speech.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: that is, you will not hear in it a word of vain talk.

It is said the meaning is lying, falsehood and disbelief. Qatadah said this, and Mujahid said: that is, reviling.

Al-Farra' said: you will not hear in it one who swears an oath with a lie.

Al-Kalbi said: you will not hear in Paradise one who swears an oath, whether righteous or sinful.

Al-Farra' also said: you will not hear in the speech of the people of Paradise a word that is vain, because they speak only with wisdom and praise of God for what He has granted them of lasting bliss. This is the most preferred of the views, because an indefinite noun in the context of negation is a form of generality, and there is no basis for restricting it to a particular kind of vain talk unless there is a specifier suitable for restriction.

*Laghiyah* is either an adjective of an omitted noun, that is, a word that is vain (*kalimah laghiyah*), or a soul that is vain (*nafs laghiyah*), or a verbal noun, that is, you will not hear in it *laghwan* (vain talk).

﴿In it is a flowing spring﴾. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Insan that in it are springs. *Al-'ayn* here means the plural *'uyun*, as in His words: ﴿A soul will know﴾ [al-Takwir: 14]. The meaning of *jariyah* (flowing) is that its waters flow and gush forth with kinds of delicious drinks.

Al-Kalbi said: I do not know whether it is water or something else.

﴿In it are raised couches﴾. That is, lofty and elevated in height, or lofty in rank.

﴿And cups set in place﴾. It has already been mentioned that *al-akwab* is the plural of *kub*, which is a cup without a handle. The meaning of *mawdu'ah* (set in place) is that they are placed before them, from which they drink.

﴿And cushions arranged in rows﴾. *Al-namariq* are cushions.

Al-Wahidi said: by the agreement of all, its singular is *numruqah* with a *damma* on the *nun*. Al-Farra' added, from Arabic hearing, *nimriqah* with a *kasra*.

Al-Kalbi said: cushions arranged in rows, some next to others. From it is the verse of the poet:

*And indeed we pass the cup among our drinkers, and between Abu Qabus, above the cushions.*

Another said:

*Elders and young men, fair of face, on couches arranged in rows, and cushions.*

In *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari) it says: *al-numruq* and *al-nimriqah* are a small cushion, and likewise *al-nimriqah* with a *kasra* is a dialectal form related by Ya'qub.

﴿And carpets spread out﴾. That is, rugs. Its singular is *zurbi* and *zurbiyyah*.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: *al-zarabi* are the thin-piled carpets (*tanafis*) with a fine nap, and its singular is *zarbiyyah*. *Mabthuthah* means spread out. So said Qatadah.

Ikrimah said: some of them are above others.

Al-Wahidi said: it may also mean that they are scattered in the gatherings. Al-Qutaybi said the same.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning of *mabthuthah* is many. The apparent meaning of *al-bath* is scattering together with abundance, and from it is His words: ﴿And He scattered throughout it from every creature﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an implied element, as in its parallels that have passed more than once. The sentence is directed to establish the matter of resurrection and to argue for it, and so is what follows. *Kayfa* is accusative, governed by what follows it. The clause is in the genitive position as a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion, a substitute that comprises part of the meaning of the noun it replaces) for *al-ibil* (the camels). The meaning is: do they deny the matter of resurrection and consider its occurrence unlikely? Do they not look at the camels, which are the mainstay of their livestock and the greatest of the created things they witness, ﴿how they were created﴾ in the wonderful form they have, with the greatness of their bodies, the abundance of their strength, and the wonder of their attributes?

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: he singled out the camels because they are among the quadrupeds that kneel, so that loads can be put on them, whereas other quadrupeds are not loaded unless they are standing. Al-Zajjaj said: He drew their attention to a great creature of His creation which He has made subservient to the little one, who leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and loads it with heavy burdens while it is kneeling. It then rises with the weight of its load, and no other load-bearing animal does this. So He showed them a great part of His creation, to indicate by it His unity.

Al-Hasan was asked about this verse, and it was said to him: the elephant is more wondrous. He said: as for the elephant, the Arabs are far removed from it. Moreover it is a pig (*khinzir*) whose back is not ridden, whose meat is not eaten, and whose milk is not milked. The camel is among the most precious and valuable property of the Arabs. It eats date-stones and fodder, produces milk, and a child takes hold of its halter and leads it wherever he wishes, despite its great size in itself.

Al-Mubarrad said: the camels here are the great clouds of the sky, but this differs from what the commentators and lexicographers mentioned.

It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: whoever reads *khuliqat* with a light pronunciation means the camel, and whoever reads it with a shadda means the clouds.

﴿And at the sky, how it was raised﴾. That is, it was raised above the earth without pillars, in a manner that understanding cannot grasp and reason cannot comprehend. It is also said: it was raised so that nothing can reach it.

﴿And at the mountains, how they were set firm﴾ upon the earth, fixed and firm, not swaying, not leaning, and not moving.

﴿And at the earth, how it was spread out﴾. That is, it was spread. *Al-sath* is the spreading of a thing. It is said of the roof of a house when it is level: *sath*.

The majority read *suthihat* in the passive voice with a light pronunciation. Al-Hasan read it with a shadda. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu al-'Aliyah read *khalaqtu, rafa'tu, nasabtu, sathahtu* (I created, I raised, I set, I spread) in the active voice with a *damma* on the *ta'* in all of them, as a first-person address from God.

Then He, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to remind, saying: ﴿So remind﴾. The *fa'* indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes. That is: so admonish them, O Muhammad, and warn them. Then He gave the reason for the command to remind, saying: ﴿You are only a reminder﴾. That is, nothing is incumbent upon you except that.

﴿You are not over them a controller﴾. *Al-musaytir* and *al-musayтир* with *sin* and *sad* mean one who is given power over a thing in order to oversee it and attend to its affairs, as stated in *al-Sihah*. That is: you are not over them a controller, so that you compel them to faith. This verse has been abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e., its ruling superseded by a later revelation) by the verse of the sword.

The majority read *bi-musaytir* with *sad*. Hisham and Qunbul in one report read it with *sin*. Khalaf read it with the *sad* pronounced as *za'* (the sound of *sad* mixed with *zay*). Harun al-A'war read it with an open *ta'* as a passive participle.

﴿Except for him who turns away and disbelieves﴾. This is an exception of disconnection (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes): that is, but as for he who turns away from admonition and reminder...

﴿فَيُعَذِّبُهُ اللَّهُ الْعَذَابَ الْأَكْبَرَ﴾ ("then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment"). This is the lasting punishment of Hell (Jahannam). It is also said that this is an exception (istithna' muttasil, a connected exception) from His saying "so remind," meaning: remind everyone except the one whose hope of his faith has been cut off and who turned away, so he deserves the greatest punishment. The first view is preferable.

It is called "the greatest" because they were already punished in this world by hunger, drought, killing and captivity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "فَإنَّهُ يُعَذِّبُهُ اللَّهُ" ("then indeed Allah will punish him"). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah recited "أَلَا مَنْ تَوَلَّى" ("Unquestionably, whoever turns away"), taking "ألا" as the particle of alerting and opening (lil-tanbih wal-istiftah).

﴿إنَّ إلَيْنا إيابَهُمْ﴾ ("Indeed, to Us is their return"), meaning their return after death. It is said: "āba yaūbu" when one returns. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"Every absent one returns, but the absent one of death does not return."

The majority read "إيابَهم" with light stress (takhfif). Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read it with a doubled letter (tashdid). Abu Hatim said: tashdid is not permissible; if it were, its equivalent would be permissible in "al-siyam" and "al-qiyam." It is also said that both are dialectal variants with the same meaning.

Al-Wahidi said: As for "إيابَهم" with a doubled yā', it is anomalous (shadh), and no one permitted it except al-Zajjaj.

﴿ثُمَّ إنَّ عَلَيْنا حِسابَهُمْ﴾ ("Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning"), meaning their recompense after their return to Allah through resurrection. "Thumma" here indicates a delay in rank, because the station of reckoning is far greater in severity than the station of return.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-Ghashiyah" is one of the names of the Resurrection.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿هَلْ أتاكَ حَدِيثُ الغاشِيَةِ﴾ ("Has there come to you the news of the Overwhelming?"), that he said: "It is the Hour." Regarding ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خاشِعَةٌ عامِلَةٌ ناصِبَةٌ﴾ ("Faces that Day will be humbled, labouring, weary"), he said: "They will labour and be weary in the Fire." Regarding ﴿تُسْقى مِن عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ﴾ ("They will be given drink from a boiling spring"), he said: "It is the one whose heat has reached its limit." Regarding ﴿لَيْسَ لَهم طَعامٌ إلّا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾ ("They will have no food except from a thorny plant"), he said: "It is al-shibriq."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: Regarding ﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ خاشِعَةٌ عامِلَةٌ ناصِبَةٌ﴾, he said: "It means the Jews and the Christians; they are humbled, but their deeds will not benefit them." Regarding ﴿تُسْقى مِن عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ﴾, he said: "Its boiling has reached its peak."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His saying ﴿تَصْلى نارًا حامِيَةً﴾ ("They will burn in a scorching Fire"), that he said: "Intensely hot." Regarding ﴿تُسْقى مِن عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ﴾, he said: "Its heat has ended." Regarding ﴿لَيْسَ لَهم طَعامٌ إلّا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾, he said: "From a tree of fire."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him also regarding ﴿إلّا مِن ضَرِيعٍ﴾, that he said: "Dried al-shibriq."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him also regarding ﴿لا تَسْمَعُ فِيها لاغِيَةً﴾ ("They will not hear therein any vain talk"), that he said: "They will not hear harm or falsehood." Regarding ﴿فِيها سُرُرٌ مَرْفُوعَةٌ﴾ ("Therein are couches raised high"), he said: "Some of them above others." Regarding ﴿ونَمارِقُ﴾ ("and cushions arranged"), he said: "Sitting places."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding ﴿ونَمارِقُ﴾, that he said: "Armrests."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding ﴿لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ﴾ ("You are not over them a controller"), that he said: "A tyrant." Regarding ﴿إلّا مَن تَوَلّى وكَفَرَ﴾ ("But whoever turns away and disbelieves"), he said: "His reckoning is upon Allah."

Abu Dawud, in his book on abrogation (al-nasikh, the verses that abrogate others), narrated from him also regarding ﴿لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُسَيْطِرٍ﴾ that this was then abrogated by His saying: ﴿فَاقْتُلُوا المُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ ("Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them") [al-Tawbah: 5].

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him also regarding ﴿إنَّ إلَيْنا إيابَهُمْ﴾ that he said: "Their return."
